'''George Albert "Jay" Keyworth II''' ('''G. A. Keyworth''') (November 30, 1939 – August 23, 2017) was an American [[physicist]] who served as [[Office of Science and Technology Policy|White House Science Advisor]] from 1981 to January 1986. He was a board member of [[Hewlett-Packard]] who was asked to step down in light of the controversy surrounding disclosure of sensitive information to the media.<ref>{{cite news | title = Dunn For? | work= [[Forbes]] | first = Parmy | last = Olsen | url = https://www.forbes.com/facesinthenews/2006/09/07/hewlett-packard-dunn-cx_po_0907autofacescan01.html | archive-url = https://archive.today/20130123083124/http://www.forbes.com/facesinthenews/2006/09/07/hewlett-packard-dunn-cx_po_0907autofacescan01.html  | archive-date = January 23, 2013 | date = 2006-09-07 | access-date = 2006-09-08 }}</ref>  He resigned on September 13, 2006.<ref name = USAToday>{{cite news | url = https://www.usatoday.com/tech/techinvestor/corporatenews/2006-09-12-hp-hurd-advantage_x.htm | title = New HP chief makes the best of a bad situation | work = [[USA Today]] | date = 2006-09-13 | access-date = 2006-09-25 | first1=Michelle | last1=Kessler | first2=Jim | last2=Hopkins}}</ref>

== Education and career ==

Keyworth attended [[Deerfield Academy]] and then received a B.S. in Physics from Yale University in 1963<ref>[https://sciencepolicy.colorado.edu/scienceadvisors/keyworth.html "Dr. George (Jay) Keyworth II"], ''Center for Science and Technology Policy Research, Policy, Politics, and Science in the White House'', [[CU-Boulder]], January 31, 2006. Retrieved 2025-03-19.</ref> and a PhD in physics from [[Duke University]] in 1968.<ref name="thesis-keyworth-1968">{{cite thesis |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/302304412/ |title=A high resolution study of isobaric analogue states in potassium-41 and sodium-23 |date=1968 |publisher=[[Duke University]] |type=Ph.D. |last=Keyworth |first=George Albert II |id={{ProQuest| }} |url-access=subscription  |oclc=21120102}}</ref>  Following the granting of his degree, he took a position at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]], where he rose to become leader of the Physics Division, the position he held when he was asked to become the presidential Science Advisor.<ref name = NYTobit/>

Keyworth was chairman and senior fellow with the [[Progress and Freedom Foundation|Progress & Freedom Foundation]] from 1995.<ref>{{cite web | title = Advisory Committee | publisher = Progress & Freedom Foundation | work = The Digital Age Communications Act Project | access-date = 2006-09-08 | url = http://www.pff.org/daca/advisorycomm.html#keyworth }}</ref><ref name = RightWeb>{{cite web | url = https://militarist-monitor.org/profile/george-kenworth/ | title = George "Jay" Keyworth II   | work = [[Militarist Monitor]] | date = February 10, 2011 | access-date = 2020-03-27 }}</ref>

Keyworth was also on the board of directors for Eon Corporation (formally known as [[TVAnswer|TV Answer]]) from 1990 to 1994.<ref>Andrews, Edmund L. (August 17, 1994). [https://www.nytimes.com/1994/08/17/business/airwave-entrepreneurs-still-feeling-their-way.html?pagewanted=3&src=pm "Airwave Entrepreneurs Still Feeling Their Way"]. ''New York Times''</ref> He worked as a liaison between TV Answer and [[Hewlett-Packard]] which eventually led to a manufacturing and marketing partnership between the two companies that was designed to speed the development of the first national interactive television system. Keyworth facilitated the agreement between HP and TV Answer to manufacture and market interactive television home units that would activate and control TV Answer's two-way system in the home.<ref>Lewyn, Mark (June 29, 1992). {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120724161659/http://www.businessweek.com/archives/1992/b3272045.arc.htm|title="This Isn't the Response TV Answer Expected"}}. ''Businessweek''</ref>

He was [[Office of Science and Technology Policy|Science Advisor]] to the President and director of the [[White House]]'s [[Office of Science and Technology Policy]] from 1981 to early 1986.<ref name = RightWeb/><ref>{{cite web | title = Past Science Advisors | work = Office of Science and Technology Policy | url = http://www.ostp.gov/html/_pastadvisors.html | access-date = 2006-09-08 }}</ref><ref name="nyt-1981may05">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1981/05/20/us/physicist-is-named-as-science-advisor.html?pagewanted=all |title=Physicist is named as science advisor |newspaper=[[New York Times]] |date=May 5, 1981 |first=Robert |last=Reinhold}}</ref> He also served as a director of General Atomics.<ref name = RightWeb/>

=== Hewlett-Packard resignation ===
In early 2005, after [[news leak]]s about then-CEO [[Carly Fiorina]]'s clashes with the board surfaced, Fiorina hired a law firm to find the source.<ref name = USAToday/>  In February 2005, Fiorina left the company and [[Patricia C. Dunn|Patricia Dunn]], non-executive chairwoman, continued the investigation.<ref name = USAToday/>  As part of a larger [[Hewlett-Packard#HP pretexting scandal|scandal]], a subcontractor used [[pretexting]] to expose Keyworth as the source of an alleged additional leak to [[CNET]], and he was outed in a May 18, 2006 board meeting.<ref name = USAToday/>  At the meeting, Dunn asked Keyworth to resign, he refused asserting that he was not the source of any unauthorized or inappropriate communication with reporters, and another board member ([[Thomas Perkins (businessman)|Tom Perkins]]) resigned over the way Keyworth was being treated.<ref name = USAToday/><ref name = SFChron>{{cite news | url = https://www.sfgate.com/business/article/hp-pushing-out-veteran-member-of-board-george-2552987.php | title = HP pushing out veteran member of board | first = Benjamin | last = Pimentel | work= [[San Francisco Chronicle]] | date = 2006-09-06 | access-date = 2006-09-25 }}</ref>  HP revealed the story on September 6, 2006, and said that they were not seeking Keyworth's reelection to the board.<ref name = SFChron/> Coinciding with [[Mark V. Hurd]]'s promotion to chairman, Keyworth resigned on September 12.<ref name = USAToday/>  In connection with Keyworth's resignation, HP made the following statement regarding the alleged CNET leak: "At HP's request, Dr. Keyworth often had contacts with the press to explain HP's interests. The board does not believe that Dr. Keyworth's contact with CNET in January 2006 was vetted through appropriate channels, but also recognizes that his discussion with the CNET reporter was undertaken in an attempt to further HP's interests. HP board chairman Patricia Dunn expressed regret for the intrusion into his privacy."<ref>[[Lesley Stahl|Stahl, Lesley]] (interviewer) and Daniel Schorn (correspondent), [https://www.cbsnews.com/news/patricia-dunn-i-am-innocent/2/ "Patricia Dunn: I Am Innocent"], CBS 60 Minutes, October 6, 2006. Editor's Note on p. 2 of 3 has press release statement. Retrieved 2020-03-27.</ref>

Keyworth had been a director of HP since 1986 and, until his resignation, was the longest-serving director at the company.<ref name = USAToday/>

==Death==
Keyworth died at his home in [[Monterey, California]] of [[prostate cancer]] on August 23, 2017, at the age of 77.<ref name = NYTobit>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/08/28/science/george-a-keyworth-ii-reagan-science-adviser-dies-at-77.html?mcubz=3|title=George A. Keyworth II, Reagan Science Adviser, Dies at 77|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=August 28, 2017|access-date=2020-03-27|quote= ... died on Wednesday ... [the Wednesday before the Monday, August 28, 2017, publication date was August 23]}}</ref>
